q1: The human (natural) language of the page. Browsers, screen readers, translation tools, and search engines all read `lang` to determine how to process and present the content.
q2: On the <html> root element. Setting it there declares the default language for the entire document. It can be overridden on individual child elements for mixed-language content.
q3: dir controls text direction. Use dir="ltr" for left-to-right languages (default) and dir="rtl" for right-to-left languages such as Arabic, Hebrew, and Persian.
q4: When a section of the page is in a different language or direction. For example, an Arabic quote inside an English page should have lang="ar" dir="rtl" on its wrapping element.
q5: Arabic and Hebrew (and also Persian/Farsi and Urdu) are written right-to-left. These scripts require dir="rtl" to render correctly.
q6: A standardised string like "en-US" or "fr". BCP 47 tags combine an ISO 639 language code with an optional ISO 3166 region subtag — for example "en" for English, "en-US" for American English.
q7: It selects the correct pronunciation engine for the language. Without the correct `lang`, a screen reader may pronounce foreign text with the wrong accent or phonetics, making it incomprehensible.
q8: It can flip margins, padding, and flex/grid direction. Setting dir="rtl" switches the logical writing direction, causing browsers to mirror layouts so they feel natural for RTL readers.
q9: To tell search engines about alternate-language versions of the page. For example, <link rel="alternate" hreflang="fr" href="/fr/page"> helps Google serve the French version to French-speaking users.
q10: Screen readers may mispronounce content; translation tools may guess wrong. The browser has to guess the language, and a wrong guess affects accessibility, SEO, and automatic translation quality.
